newsitem.title: USA: Whirlpool says results will be lower.
newsitem.headline: Whirlpool says results will be lower.

text.p: Whirlpool Corp. said Friday a surprisingly sluggish market in western Europe could depress its third-quarter results by as much as 40 percent before restructuring costs from a year earlier.
Whirlpool, the world's largest maker of major home appliances, said the problems in Europe, the firm's second-largest regional market, prompted it to lower its full-year expectations.

The Benton Harbour, Mich.-based company also said it plans to take a $30 million restructuring charge in the third quarter for the previously announced streamlining of its Asian headquarters and a North American refrigeration operation.

Whirlpool Chairman David Whitwam said year-to-date results from the company's North American and Latin American operations are at record levels. He added both regions are expected to perform strongly through the rest of the year.
Following the announcement, Whirlpool stock tumbled $1.625 to $50.50 on the New York Stock Exchange.
The news caused a round of earnings estimate cuts from analysts.

"This is another in a series of earnings disappointments in the past five quarters," said Merrill Lynch analyst Jonathan Goldfarb. "The fact is that this whole aggressive global diversification campaign just doesn't seem to be working."
Goldfarb said he now expects Whirlpool to report 1996 per hare earnings of $2.25, down from his previous estimate of $2.90. In all of 1995, Whirlpool earned $209 million, or $2.80 a share.
The company said the difficult economic environment in Europe will lead to a small quarterly operating loss at Whirlpool Europe, following a second-quarter loss there.
Europe contributed about 30 percent of Whirlpool's $8.16 billion in annual appliance sales for 1995. North America is the company's largest market, with $5.09 billion in revenues last year.

Although the company now also expects to have another loss in its Asian operations, it was the European operations news that most troubled analysts. At its annual analyst gathering in January, the company signalled that its European operations would be stronger in 1996.

Susan Gallagher, an analyst at NatWest Securities Corp., said Europe remains a difficult place to do business as governments grapple with social welfare costs, unemployment stays high and consumers are cautious in their spending.
"There is no pricing ability to speak of," she said.

Whirlpool spokesman T.R. Reid said Whirlpool's unit shipments to Europe will be up when the industry as a whole will be down slightly. Meantime, he said increasing competition demands that the company pursue its global diversification.
"This isn't a short-term strategy. It's a long-term strategy and, we think, absolutely the right strategy," he said.
